title: the work is the medicine you need
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

this is about trusting in the work you need, and how creating from necessity is a form of creative power, because it keeps you close to what's vital, alive, and electric -- more than any "should" energy ever could.

I'll explore how generative discomfort can be used as fuel for excavating creative potential, and how to sense into what's ready to be metabolized -- into medicine. I'll share concrete examples from my 11 years of obsessions, and leave you with questions to contemplate.

⁠the process is the way⁠

Today's episode is inspired by a phrase that's kept coming up in my mind these recent weeks: "The work is the medicine you need."

Whenever I create something new, a podcast, a new course, an offering, I'm never really asking myself what would be strategic, what do other people want, what would sell. Instead, I'm asking myself, what do I most need right now? What feels the most necessary for me? What process of metabolizing or distilling do I need to go through in this moment, in this season of my life?

This sounds like a pretty self-centered business creative strategy, but I find that whenever I center in the work that feels absolutely essential for me, what I create will always have more generative energy, more aliveness, more electricity. When the work isn't optional, when the work feels so necessary, like medicine for you to be well, that's when it feels most vital and deeply connected to a sense of life purpose.

So today I want to talk about how I'm thinking about the words medicine and work as practice and process. I want to explore how generative discomfort can be creative fuel for making the work. Why is it that necessity creates power? And share some concrete examples from my life as well as a process for thinking about this work.

reframing medicine

In this episode, the way I'll be using the words medicine and healing is as process and practice. So not saying that any of us are inherently sick or wounded or broken, but that the experience of being human is inherently full of pain and suffering and discomfort.

For example, allowing oneself to be seen is hard. Visibility is hard and often comes from a lifetime of conditioning and early experiences that left imprints on our psyche. Trusting one's creative instincts is so hard. Doing something different than what we were raised to do is hard and feels often impossible sometimes to let go of old patterns. We need resistance every step of the way. We confront our vulnerabilities and our wounds every step of the way.

So medicine is anything that is a salve for those forms of difficulty, for the resistance that we encounter on the creative path. Your creative work is medicine. Showing up to make the work, share the work is medicine. Weaving a business that feels true and authentic to your energy is medicine.

Medicine is not a one-time thing that you ingest and be done with and be totally healed. It's often something that you don't completely understand how it works, the mechanics of it. You allow the process to be metabolized in your body. You allow it to work through you and you have to trust the medicine. You have to surrender to it.

Sometimes this can feel very uncomfortable facing the fear of being rejected, facing the fear of silence in the digital void, of leaving social media, of imposter syndrome. All of that is medicine if you see it that way. It will bring up so much dirt and shadows and wounds from the past and it can be nourishing. It can feel like eating whole foods. It can feel cleansing. It can feel even pleasurable. It's a delayed kind of pleasure and acquired taste.

Medicine is anything that allows you to heal and change and evolve in the direction of your intentions.

generative discomfort

So when I say that the work is the medicine, I mean to sense into what parts of your work create generative discomfort. Where do you feel friction, tension, resistance, intensity? And how can you see those places as sources of your power as geysers of creative potential, juicy and rich?

I'm thinking about how in astrological terms, Chiron is the wounded healer and how the healing work that we do often comes from our deepest wounds. My Chiron is in Leo in the 10th house, which is all about career, being visible, being seen in the public role, being a leader. And yeah, that's terrifying for me, but here I am. This is my work and my medicine.

And personally, I like to pick at the wounds that I feel. I like to process raw pain through art, through writing, but I don't necessarily recommend the strategy for everyone. Not all pain is creative fuel, nor is it ready to become fuel. Sometimes certain kinds of pain is much too raw. And in those cases, it might need something different, external support, therapy, time, spaciousness.

So key to this practice is discernment, tuning into your capacity. What work, what topics or themes in your life are you ready to make medicine out of through a process of alchemy? And what needs to be left alone or have more time?

This is why I'm using the word generative discomfort to describe the work that feels malleable and workable, the kind of discomfort and pain that you feel excited to obsess over, to turn into something, where making the work could feel like a powerful salve and not something that keeps you frozen or stuck or paralyzed.

So this is kind of like finding a good vein, like the vein is ready for you, and practice listening to it, sensing into it, leaning into it, very gently, very softly, one day at a time. You could also think of it as like kneading dough. You knead it and you let it sit and rise. You step away and then you come back to it and sense how the structure and form has changed. Patience is absolutely key.


necessity creates power

The core premise here is that necessity creates power. The work that feels the most necessary is often the hardest and the most powerful.

I often swing from avoidance to obsession. I find that the things which I avoid will always come back, not to haunt me, but to present themselves as if on a conveyor belt to say, "I'm almost ready for you. I'm ready to be metabolized. I'm ready to receive your attention."

The work which I avoid the most, which feels challenging to me, not neutral, not indifferent, those other places where I have the most potential for growth, where there's the most richness there to be excavated, and this might take years for it to be ready. There is no rush to work through every area of stuckness or resistance. Each area of discomfort has its own timeline.

And sometimes this can be an acute event. For example, I had a recent life rupture, and I spent many weeks just drawing a lot in my sketchbook as creative medicine for this period of time, or this could be a slow accumulation over years. For example, I just taught a class on money after four years of intensely doing money work, and the class felt like bottling hard-earned lessons for my past and future selves.

I make something to be the medicine I need across dimensions of time, because I go in circles. Sometimes I forget what I learned five years ago, and I need to be reminded, or sometimes I make work that is like making something for a past version of myself. Many of my students in my courses feel like past versions of me that I'm speaking to with as much tenderness and compassion as possible.

Therefore, it's essential that the work I create has a necessity, has a vitality to it. I can't not create it. And so necessity creates power, because if I don't do this work, I'm not fulfilling an authentic part of who I am. I'll either feel mild discomfort, or it'll escalate into anxiety spirals and existential despair.

I learned early in my life that emotions can feel so extreme and all-consuming that the mind can feel like a tornado, and the only way out of those inner world mental states is to focus on a vision, a feeling, a future that I want to create through the things that I make in my work, to make the work that can help carry me forwards.

And I think when you make work from that feeling of necessity, survival, and I don't just mean body survival, but soul survival, survival as the most essential part of you, there's a quality of fierceness to the work. The work is created through a need to take responsibility. The authority with which you make this work comes from a real place.

And of course, this can feel really vulnerable. How do other people respond to this work? What if nobody likes it? Well, that's part of the medicine as well. You make the work because you need to make the work, not because there's someone on the other side offering validation for it.

becoming the example

When you make the work that is the most essential to you, you're tending to where there is pain, discomfort, friction, resistance. You become a walking example of your own work in process. You become a channel for the wisdom moving through you. You become an inspiration for other people who are grappling with the same things, who have experienced the same pain.

And I think the more that you share your journey with them as a process rather than an end result of happily ever after, the more that it creates a living connection with them. The world hurts all of us in similar ways. And part of the work is sharing our medicines with each other. You become the light after walking through darkness.

my timeline: 11 years of obsessions

To give you some examples of my obsessions over the last 11 years, I graduated college and I spent seven years just writing about wellbeing, the inner world and creative practices. I was working a nine to five job. I was constantly overwhelmed by my own emotions that I didn't understand by my anxiety. And I just decided to write about it, write about art and creative process and metabolize my life and share it on my website. I was making my own medicine for how to recenter myself as a moody creative person and how to make their creative work even when there's no one paying attention.

Then in 2022, I looked at those seven years of writing and sharing, and I zoomed out to see what I was doing. And I realized that I was building a world of my own on the internet, on my website. So I started writing about digital ecosystems and world building and sort of articulating my frameworks and philosophies. I was making the medicine of, this is how you share your work without needing social media or do things that feel inauthentic. This is how you make a home on the internet that can feel true to you.

Then in 2023, I started writing a lot about building a business as an artist. By that point, I had already been working for seven years with private clients. I had spent three years teaching courses. It was a very cyclical process of starting and stopping and making tons of mistakes. I could feel where there was resistance and pain, and I could articulate medicine that was a salve for that resistance.

I could bottle the medicine of, this is how art and business can be integrated. This is how I can heal my relationship with money and making money. This is how I can decompartmentalize the schizophrenia that I felt between my artist self and business self. And this is how I can inhabit my power in the material world as an artist.

And so my four threads, my four themes are inner world wellbeing practices, creative process, digital ecosystems and world building and growing a business as an artist. These four themes did not emerge fully formed. I obsessed over each theme for years through daily digestion, processing, making the work, sharing the work, writing a fragment of a thought on my website, knowing that probably no one would ever read it until one day they did.

This happened over a very long period of time. In this process, I went through an enormous transformation. I made the medicine that I most needed because it was the only way I felt like my soul, my creative spirit could survive. And as it turns out, I am not alone. The more that I do this work, the more that I realize that I'm not the only person who needs it.


process of making medicine

So let's talk about the process. I'll refer you back to episode seven, "The Process is the Way," which is a master key, I think to doing any kind of work. Crucial here is that if you have any challenge or any problem that you're trying to solve, an essential skill is knowing how to identify where the resistance is, what is pulling you towards it and what is creating the friction. In that push and pull, there is the generative discomfort.

This is you finding the vein and knowing that maybe it's not ready yet. Maybe it'll give you signals and signs, or maybe it is and you just need to be patient with it. Maybe it's something that you're ready to explore in the intimacy of your own journals or sketchbooks, or maybe it's ready to be explored publicly and shared on your website, in your newsletters, or maybe it's ready to be metabolized and distilled into an offering.

All of these are forms of medicine. Creative work is medicine, sharing the work is medicine and guiding other people through this work is medicine.

When I think about the arc of how making medicine unfolds, it always starts with sensing into the generative discomfort, choosing to take responsibility, feeling ready to do something about it, not trying to avoid it, not running away, maybe asking it, what does it want to be? What creative form does it want to be poured into? Allowing myself to be guided by the creative process, that working with raw material is like having a dance with life or wrestling with the magical sea octopus or letting myself wander out into the dark forest and staying present through all of it, trusting myself that I have the resources to create what I most need, that I will be transformed in some small ways, perhaps on the other side.

This doesn't happen overnight. It happens one tiny step at a time.

I started this year off with a three-part mini series. "Make the Work, Share the Work" is about creating the medicine. "Make an Offering, Weave the Web" is about evolving an ecosystem around the medicine. And "Make Art the Center of Your World" is seeing art as medicine, art as about digesting life, as soul water.

The Invitation

Today, I'm inviting you to see how work that comes from necessity also has the most power. Think about the places in your life where you feel discomfort that is creatively generative. Where does friction and resistance spark something in you that feels alive and ready and malleable to be worked with?

And again, this doesn't mean you need to share it right away. It doesn't mean you need to make it into a business or monetize it, but it does mean you would choose to prioritize this work. You would trust in the long process of metabolizing it, and maybe this takes days, weeks, months, or maybe it takes years.

This is about not running away from the hard places and instead letting it become creative fuel for making the creative medicine that is the most life-giving, not only for yourself now, but for your past self, for your future selves, and for so many other souls in this world because we are never alone, because the personal is the universal. And so making something that is truly a salve for your specific discomfort and pain will no doubt be a salve for others.

Trust in the process and know that this is something that unfolds over time.

Closing

Thank you for listening to this episode. If you'd like to explore creative practice and process with my guidance and the support of a community, I invite you to join Labyrinth Library. The next season will start on Monday.

If you're looking for a more structured curriculum to reimagine a business, I'm teaching my capstone course, Digital Abundance, live starting in early March. I just finished teaching Money Juice Cleanse which is definitely the medicine that I needed for doing money work. You can explore all of these in the show notes.

The best way to keep in touch with me is through my newsletter. I invite you to explore my website where you can explore my other writings, courses, and working with me one-on-one.

Until next time.
